typhoon.title: Typhoon, earthquake & autumn weather
typhoon.note: Late Oct–Nov is the tail of typhoon season, and Japan is earthquake-prone year-round. Know your hotel's evacuation info, keep your phone charged, and turn on emergency alerts.
items: Typhoons: trains may pre-emptively suspend service ('keikaku unkyū') — check operator sites and don't travel toward a landfall.
Earthquakes: drop, cover, hold on; move away from windows; follow staff and announcements. Aftershocks are normal.
Enable Japan's emergency alerts on your phone; NHK World and the Japan Meteorological Agency (jma.go.jp) publish English updates.
Install JNTO's free 'Safety tips' app for English disaster push-alerts.

restaurants.name: Gyudon chains (Yoshinoya / Sukiya / Matsuya)
restaurants.detail: Beef-bowl chains are the backbone of cheap daily eating. Regular gyudon runs ~¥400-600 (small ~¥400, large ~¥600). Matsuya uses a ticket vending machine at the door; Sukiya/Yoshinoya often have table or counter ordering. Open ~24h at many branches, so they cover late nights after gigs/arcades. Curry, breakfast sets, and miso soup combos keep a full meal under ¥700.
restaurants.how_or_when: No reservation. Walk in anytime. At Matsuya buy a meal ticket from the machine first (English available); hand stub to staff. IC card (Suica/PASMO) accepted at most.

restaurants.name: Standing soba/udon at train stations (tachigui)
restaurants.detail: Stand-and-slurp soba counters inside or beside stations serve a hot bowl in ~90 seconds for ¥300-500. Kake soba (plain) is cheapest; add kakiage (fritter) or tempura for ~¥150 more. A genuinely good budget meal and a daily-commute staple. Notable: Fuji Soba (chain, many 24h), plus platform stands on JR lines.
restaurants.how_or_when: No reservation, no seats. Buy ticket from vending machine, hand to counter, eat standing within minutes. Peak commuter rushes (8am, 6-7pm) get crowded but move fast.
restaurants.area_or_park: Inside/adjacent to most JR and metro stations

restaurants.name: Conveyor-belt sushi (Sushiro / Kura / Hama)
restaurants.detail: Kaiten-zushi chains start around ¥120-150 per plate (prices rose past the old ¥100 line). Most diners eat 8-15 plates for roughly ¥800-1,800. Touchscreen ordering (English/multilingual) sends plates directly to your seat; Kura Sushi gamifies it with a capsule-toy prize every 5 plates. Great for solo software-work breaks.
restaurants.how_or_when: Weekends/dinner: book a slot via the chain's own app (Sushiro app, EPARK for Kura) to skip 60-90 min waits; otherwise take a numbered ticket from the lobby kiosk and wait for your number on screen. Weekday lunch is usually walk-in.
restaurants.area_or_park: Citywide; large branches in Shibuya, Ikebukuro, suburbs

restaurants.name: Saizeriya (cheap Italian-style family chain)
restaurants.detail: Beloved budget Italian: pasta, doria, pizza, and the famous ~¥300 free-refill drink bar. Many dishes ¥300-500; a full plate-plus-drink lunch lands under ¥800. Comfortable booths, free Wi-Fi at many branches, and a tolerant attitude to lingering make it a low-key remote-work or study spot. Order via the paper checklist or table tablet.
restaurants.how_or_when: No reservation. Walk in; for groups put your name on the lobby list. Avoid 12-1pm weekday rush if you want a quiet work seat.

restaurants.name: Supermarket / depachika half-price (han-gaku) bento & sushi
restaurants.detail: The single best WHV money-saver. Supermarkets (Life, Ito-Yokado, Maruetsu, Seiyu) and department-store food halls slap yellow/red discount stickers on prepared bento, sushi, sashimi, and deli items as closing approaches. Discounts typically start ~5pm and deepen to 30-50% off after 8pm. A ¥600 sushi tray becomes ¥300. Stack with point cards.
restaurants.how_or_when: No booking. Arrive 7:30-9pm near closing; look for 半額 (half) / 〇〇円引き (yen-off) stickers. Best selection mid-evening, deepest cuts just before close.
restaurants.area_or_park: Local supermarkets near your apartment; depachika at Shinjuku/Ikebukuro stations

restaurants.name: Izakaya (after-work drinking & small plates)
restaurants.detail: The core social-dining format and your best path for meetups/conventions afterparties. Order rounds of small plates (yakitori, karaage, sashimi, edamame) plus drinks; budget ~¥3,000-4,500/person with a couple of drinks. Watch for the otoshi (compulsory ~¥300-500 seating snack/cover charge) added automatically. Chains (Torikizoku ~¥390/item, Watami) are cheap and reliable; independent izakaya in Shinjuku Omoide Yokocho or Ebisu are atmospheric.
restaurants.how_or_when: Walk-in for chains; for Friday nights or groups 4+, book via Tabelog or the izakaya's own line. As a WHV holder you'll have a Japanese phone + residence card within weeks — call or use the JAPANESE Tabelog flow to dodge the foreigner credit-card requirement. Nomihodai (all-you-can-drink, ~90-120 min) packages must usually be reserved ahead.

restaurants.name: Must-try ramen: Fuunji, Rokurinsha, Nakiryu, Afuri, Ichiran
restaurants.detail: A ramen tour worth doing: Fuunji (Shinjuku) — intense fish-pork tsukemen, arguably the city's best dipping ramen; Rokurinsha (Tokyo Station Ramen Street) — legendary tsukemen, lunch lines of salarymen; Nakiryu (Otsuka) — Michelin-starred tan-tan-men & tsukemen; Afuri (Ebisu/Harajuku) — light yuzu-shio, great entry bowl; Ichiran (Shibuya etc.) — solo tonkotsu booths, fully customizable, tourist-famous but fun once. Bowls ¥1,000-1,600.
restaurants.how_or_when: No reservations anywhere — it's queue culture. Buy a meal ticket from the vending machine at the door, then wait. Go off-peak (right at open ~11am, or 2-3pm) to cut 30-60 min lines at Fuunji/Rokurinsha/Nakiryu. Cash often needed at smaller shops.
restaurants.area_or_park: Shinjuku, Tokyo Station, Otsuka, Ebisu/Harajuku, Shibuya

restaurants.name: Pokémon Cafe (Nihonbashi)
restaurants.detail: Reopened June 17, 2026 after renovation, with strict advance-only web reservations — no day-of walk-ins. Character-themed plates and drinks; the appeal is the experience and exclusive merch, not the food value (expect ~¥2,000-3,500/person plus souvenir cup add-ons). Weekend slots vanish within minutes of release.
restaurants.how_or_when: Book on the official site exactly 31 days in advance at 12:00 (noon) JST — set an alarm and be logged in early. Window noted as opening one month ahead; weekend slots fill in minutes. Verify the exact release time on the official page before your target date.

restaurants.name: Square Enix Cafe (Akihabara) & maid cafes
restaurants.detail: Square Enix Cafe in Akihabara rotates Final Fantasy / Kingdom Hearts / Dragon Quest themed menus and merch in seasonal runs, using advance web booking like Pokémon Cafe — directly on-theme for your games/anime interests. Separately, Akihabara maid cafes (Maidreamin, @home cafe) are walk-in entertainment with a per-hour cover charge plus per-item pricing; treat as a novelty experience, not a meal.
restaurants.how_or_when: Square Enix Cafe: reserve online in advance when a new title-season opens (check official Square Enix Cafe page for the booking window). Maid cafes: walk in; expect a time-limited seating + cover charge and photo fees.
restaurants.price_or_cost: Square Enix ~¥1,500-3,000 + merch; maid cafes cover ~¥700-1,000 + items

restaurants.name: Omakase / sushi splurge — booking via OMAKASE, Pocket Concierge, TableCheck
restaurants.detail: Three English platforms are the foreigner-friendly path to counter omakase and Michelin tables, all accepting foreign Visa/Mastercard. OMAKASE (omakase.in) — counter sushi/kaiseki/tempura/yakiniku, official Michelin Guide partner; ~¥390/seat booking fee plus FULL course prepayment. Pocket Concierge (Amex-owned) — high-end, prepay the full course at booking; narrower list. TableCheck — broadest, usually just a credit-card hold (~¥200) rather than full prepay. Expect course prices ¥15,000-40,000+ at top sushi-ya.
restaurants.how_or_when: Book popular spots 2-4 weeks ahead; Michelin-starred 2-3 months ahead, the moment the booking calendar opens. Create accounts now and watch release dates. Prepaid bookings are non-refundable inside the cancellation window — diarize it.

restaurants.name: The foreigner-reservation problem & your WHV workaround
restaurants.detail: Many top restaurants got burned by foreigner no-shows, so English bookings now demand a credit card and some shops won't take overseas reservations at all (locals/concierge only). Key 2026 change: Tabelog launched a multilingual reservation app (Nov 17, 2025) where credit-card registration is MANDATORY in the English flow — but the JAPANESE-language flow often lets you book with no card. YOUR ADVANTAGE: as a WHV resident you'll get a Japanese phone number and residence card within weeks, so you can use the Japanese Tabelog/phone path and the friendly walk-in treatment locals get. For phone-only shops, options: ask a hotel/host concierge to call, or use a paid agent (TABLEALL ~¥8,000/seat). Always honor or cancel early — no-shows are why this friction exists.
restaurants.how_or_when: Set up a Japanese SIM/number and learn the Japanese Tabelog flow early in your stay. For phone-only Michelin spots, use a concierge or TABLEALL. Cancel well before the cutoff to avoid fees and protect your standing.
restaurants.price_or_cost: Free via Japanese flow / phone; paid agent ~¥8,000/seat

restaurants.name: Ohashi (大はし) — Kita-Senju
restaurants.detail: A Kita-Senju institution: a ~130-year-old izakaya famous for niku-dōfu (slow-simmered beef and tofu) and a deeply old-Tokyo atmosphere — counted among 'Tokyo's three great nikomi' izakaya. Order the nikomi (simmered offal) and a cold one.
restaurants.how_or_when: Near Kita-Senju Station. Opens late afternoon; can queue — go early. Cash-friendly.

restaurants.name: Sasaya — motsuyaki, Kita-Senju
restaurants.detail: A classic Kita-Senju motsuyaki (grilled offal skewers) joint — smoky, cheap, convivial standing-bar energy. The kushiyaki and boiled-offal skewers (kushinikomi) are the move. Pure north-Tokyo shitamachi vibe.
restaurants.how_or_when: Kita-Senju izakaya streets. Evenings; expect a wait at peak. Cash.

restaurants.name: Tanaka Shōten (田中商店) — tonkotsu ramen, Adachi
restaurants.detail: A beloved Adachi ramen shop doing rich, Hakata-style tonkotsu with thin straight noodles — the negi-chāshū bowl (heaps of green onion + slightly salty chāshū) is the favourite. Worth the trip for ramen heads.
restaurants.how_or_when: Near Nishiarai / Ōyata, Adachi. Lunch and dinner; ticket machine. Cash.

restaurants.detail: A ~20-seat second-floor Dogenzaka listening bar where owner Kobayashi-san spins from a wall of 10,000+ jazz, blues and soul records on a warm tube system — the archetypal Tokyo one-man vinyl bar.
restaurants.how_or_when: Opens in the afternoon and runs into the evening, so it works as a daytime stop too; go solo or as a pair, keep your voice low, and don't photograph the records — cash only, no reservations.
restaurants.name: JBS (Jazz, Blues, Soul)

restaurants.detail: A 1926-founded classical-music kissa in a baroque two-storey hall where every seat faces a wall of giant speakers like a cinema of sound — talking loudly and phones are banned, you just sit with coffee and a symphony.
restaurants.how_or_when: Open daily roughly 11:00-22:30; go on a weekday afternoon for a quiet seat, order at your table, and note there are set 'concert' request times — no photos inside, cash only.
restaurants.price_or_cost: Coffee ~¥700-900, one drink per person expected
restaurants.name: Meikyoku Kissa Lion

restaurants.detail: A no-seats tachigui (standing) sushi counter run by a fish wholesaler, so you get market-fresh nigiri made to order at a fraction of sit-down prices — perfect fast solo dinner before a Shibuya gig.
restaurants.how_or_when: Open from ~11:30 through late evening; order piece by piece from the chef or grab a set, expect 20-30 minutes on your feet, no reservations — avoid the 12-13:00 office rush.
restaurants.price_or_cost: ~¥75-300 per nigiri pair; a solid meal ¥1,500-2,500
restaurants.name: Uogashi Nihon-Ichi (Shibuya Dogenzaka)

restaurants.detail: One of Tokyo's benchmark old-school kissaten: hand-poured nel-drip coffee served in porcelain the master picks to match your order, plus a famous chiffon cake, in a hushed wood-and-copper room minutes from Shibuya's chaos.
restaurants.how_or_when: Open daily roughly 11:00-23:00; expect a short queue on weekends — go on a weekday mid-afternoon, order the aged blend or a nel-drip single origin, cash preferred.
restaurants.name: Chatei Hatou

disney.name: Fantasy Springs entry: no area gate, but rides need Standby Pass (free) OR DPA (paid)
disney.detail: Fantasy Springs (DisneySea's newest land: Frozen Kingdom, Rapunzel's Lantern Festival, Peter Pan's Never Land Adventure) currently has NO area-entry restriction. The app shows 'You can enter at any time' when no cap is in place. BUT to ride any of the 3 rides you MUST hold either a free Standby Pass (timed, app-issued, then you queue) or paid Disney Premier Access. The old virtual-queue/Entry Request lottery system ended. Capacity caps can return on peak days, so check the Park Ticket screen in the app on arrival. Strategy: pull a Standby Pass the moment you tap in at the gate, then ride others via DPA or repeat Standby Passes.
disney.how_or_when: In the Tokyo Disney Resort app: 'Standby Pass' and 'Disney Premier Access' tabs. New Standby Pass available 2 hours after your last; new DPA available 1 hour after your last. You can hold one of each simultaneously. Pull-to-refresh through the day as more slots release.
disney.price_or_cost: Standby Pass free; DPA paid (see DPA item)

disney.name: Disney Premier Access (DPA) — paid skip-the-line, dynamic per-ride pricing
disney.detail: DPA is per-person, per-attraction, bought in-app on the day. Dynamic pricing: ¥1,500–¥2,500 depending on ride and crowd. DisneySea: Frozen Kingdom / Rapunzel / Peter Pan (Fantasy Springs) ¥2,000–2,500; Soaring, Toy Story Mania, Tower of Terror ¥1,500–2,000; Journey to the Center of the Earth ~¥1,500; premium shows (Believe! Sea of Dreams, Dance the Globe) up to ¥2,500. Disneyland: Beauty and the Beast ¥1,500–2,500; Baymax, Big Thunder Mountain, Pooh's Hunny Hunt ¥1,500–2,000; Buzz Lightyear ~¥1,500. Space Mountain unavailable (closed for the rebuild). Sources differ on whether the second-DPA gap is a strict 1 hour or 'after you scan' — treat 1 hour as the safe assumption.
disney.how_or_when: Buy in the app on the day. Buy a new DPA 1 hour after the previous one (or after scanning, per some sources). A QR code generates instantly; scan at the Premier Access entrance in your time window. For a synth/games-focused solo trip, spend DPA only on the 3 Fantasy Springs headliners + Soaring; use free Standby Pass / early rope-drop for the rest.

disney.name: 1-Day Passport pricing — date-specific, variable (weekday vs weekend/peak)
disney.detail: Adult 1-Day 1-Park Passport runs roughly ¥7,900 (cheapest weekdays) to ¥10,900 (peak weekends/holidays). Junior ~¥6,600–9,000, Child ~¥4,700–5,600. Price is tied to the specific date you choose — Tokyo Disney does NOT do open-dated gate tickets and does NOT sell at the gate. Moving a Saturday plan to a Tue/Wed midweek date saves ¥2,000–3,000 per adult AND gives shorter lines. As a 12-month WHV resident you have huge flexibility — always pick a cheap-tier weekday.
disney.how_or_when: Tier/price for a given date appears on the official ticket calendar ~2 months out. Pick lowest-tier midweek dates outside school breaks.

disney.name: Online ticket buying window — open ~2 months (60 days) ahead, date-specific
disney.detail: Fixed-date tickets release for purchase about 2 months (60 days) in advance on the official site/app. Booking exactly at the 60-day mark at 2:00 PM Japan time gives the widest selection; weekends and event days can sell out. Buy via: official Tokyo Disney Resort website/app (needs a MyDisney account — tickets auto-link), Klook (QR code you scan into the app), or — once in Japan — 7-Eleven/Lawson/FamilyMart convenience-store machines. No gate sales.
disney.how_or_when: Set a reminder for ~60 days before your target date; buy at 14:00 JST. Link to the app immediately so the QR lives on your phone.

disney.name: Tokyo Disney Resort app — mandatory toolkit, set up BEFORE the gate
disney.detail: The app is non-negotiable: it holds your ticket QR (scanned at the gate), real-time wait times, show schedules, park map, restaurant menus + mobile dining orders, Standby Pass, DPA, and the free Entry Request lottery for parades/shows/character greetings. Download and link all tickets before you fly; create a MyDisney account. CRITICAL gotcha: you need working mobile data inside the park or the app is dead weight — as a WHV resident, get a Japanese SIM/eSIM early (don't rely on tourist data). The first 30 minutes after opening are when Standby Passes/DPA move fastest, so be logged in and ready at the gate.
disney.how_or_when: Set up the night before. App Store / Google Play 'Tokyo Disney Resort App'. Have data + battery bank.

disney.name: Cheapest + least-crowded days — Tue/Wed/Thu, avoid peaks
disney.detail: Best value AND shortest lines: Tuesday–Thursday, outside school breaks. Saturday and Friday are busiest; Monday is a busier weekday. Quietest windows in your 12 months: mid-Sept to early Nov (after Obon, before Christmas season) and late Jan to mid-Feb (after New Year, before spring break). June (your arrival month) and July are also relatively quiet. AVOID: Golden Week (late Apr–early May, an extreme global peak), Obon (mid-Aug), Christmas/New Year (Dec 27–Jan 3), and Feb-late/March spring breaks. A cheap-tier weekday stacks the savings (lower ticket price) with the experience (lower waits = less DPA spend needed).
disney.how_or_when: Target Tue/Wed/Thu in your first weeks (early–mid July is quiet) and again Sept–Oct. Cross-check a crowd calendar (queue-times.com, thrill-data.com, TDR Explorer) before booking.
disney.price_or_cost: Saves ¥2,000–3,000/ticket vs weekend + less DPA needed

disney.name: DisneySea 25th Anniversary 'Sparkling Jubilee' — the headline event of your whole stay
disney.detail: Runs Apr 15, 2026 – Mar 31, 2027, so it covers essentially your ENTIRE 12-month window (you land June 30, 2026). Signature color 'Jubilee Blue', anniversary décor, special merch, and new shows. Tie-ins to plan around: 'Dance the Globe' (debuts Jan 14, 2026) — 25-min music/dance show at Waterfront Park, 2–4x/day; 'D-Groovationz4 Live' concert-style show debuts Sept 30, 2026 at Showbase, Tomorrowland (strong fit for your music interest); plus the DisneySea Food & Wine Festival ('travel the world through cuisine'). Anniversary merch and limited shows sell out — go early in your stay and revisit, since you have the whole year.
disney.how_or_when: Apr 15, 2026–Mar 31, 2027. Hit it on a quiet weekday; book anniversary shows via Entry Request lottery or DPA in-app on the day.
disney.price_or_cost: Included with park admission; premium shows DPA ¥2,500

disney.name: Disney Halloween 2026 — Sept 16–Oct 31
disney.detail: Runs Sept 16 – Oct 31, 2026 at both parks. Special parades/shows, seasonal food, merch, and full-costume days for guests on designated dates. Falls in one of the year's quieter, cheaper windows (mid-Sept to early Nov), so it's a sweet spot: festive atmosphere without peak prices or peak crowds. Great early target since you'll be settled in Tokyo by then.
disney.how_or_when: Sept 16–Oct 31, 2026. Pick a Tue/Wed/Thu. Included with admission. Dates are official/annual-pattern but confirm exact 2026 dates on the official events page closer.

disney.name: Disney Christmas 2026 — Nov 11–Dec 25
disney.detail: Runs Nov 11 – Dec 25, 2026 at both parks: Christmas trees, illuminations, seasonal parades/shows, food and merch. Beautiful but November is one of the most popular months and December gets crowded as it builds toward the holidays — pricing tiers run high. Go on a weekday early in the window (mid-Nov) rather than the Dec 27–Jan 3 New Year crush. DisneySea's harbor illuminations pair with the 25th Anniversary décor this year.
disney.how_or_when: Nov 11–Dec 25, 2026. Weekday in mid-to-late Nov is the value pick; avoid the last 10 days before Christmas. Included with admission.
disney.price_or_cost: Included; expect high ticket tiers on these dates

disney.name: Vacation Packages — the only way to GUARANTEE Fantasy Springs rides (skip the pass scramble)
disney.detail: A Tokyo Disney Resort Vacation Package bundles an on-site hotel + dated park tickets + perks. The killer perk: the 2-day 'Enjoy Attractions Even More' plan includes a Fantasy Springs Magic pass giving unlimited Fantasy Springs area access AND Premier Access to all 3 Fantasy Springs rides — no Standby Pass scramble, no per-ride DPA fees. Also includes selectable hotel (Fantasy Springs Hotel, MiraCosta, Disneyland Hotel, Ambassador, Toy Story Hotel), popcorn bucket voucher, original-goods voucher, beverage ticket, and pre-bookable character-greeting times. Expensive vs a day ticket, but if you want guaranteed Fantasy Springs without app stress, this is the lever. As a year-long resident you can splurge once and DIY the rest.
disney.how_or_when: Book in advance via the official Vacation Package site (reserve.tokyodisneyresort.jp). Packages open further ahead than day tickets and sell out — book well in advance (think months, especially for Fantasy Springs Hotel). Verify current package tiers/pricing closer.
disney.price_or_cost: Splurge — hotel + tickets + perks bundle (varies by hotel/date)

disney.name: Disney Hotel 'Happy Entry' — early-entry edge for Fantasy Springs
disney.detail: Guests staying at the four Tokyo Disney Resort Disney Hotels (incl. Fantasy Springs Hotel, MiraCosta, Disneyland Hotel, Ambassador) get 'Happy Entry' — admission ~15 minutes before official opening on their checkout day at the corresponding park. With Fantasy Springs now on a first-come Standby Pass system, that head start materially improves your odds of grabbing early Standby Passes / riding before the crowd. Fantasy Springs Hotel guests get the strongest Fantasy Springs access. A one-night on-site stay is a tactical splurge to nail the hard-to-ride headliners.
disney.how_or_when: Stay at a Disney Hotel; Happy Entry applies on checkout day at the matching park. Confirm exact lead-time minutes and eligible park on the official page when booking.

disney.name: Free Entry Request lottery — parades, shows & character greetings
disney.detail: Entry Request is a FREE in-app lottery for designated parades, shows, and character greetings (separate from paid DPA). You request a slot; if you win, you get an assigned viewing area/time. For the 25th Anniversary shows and seasonal Halloween/Christmas entertainment, this is how you secure good spots without paying. Budget-friendly counterpart to DPA — use it aggressively. Note it's a lottery, not guaranteed, so have a backup plan.
disney.how_or_when: In the app's 'Entry Request' section once you're in the park. Request early in the day; results are instant. Free.

activities.name: Kameari — Kochikame statues + Ario mall (your nearest fun, 1 stop away)
activities.detail: Kameari is the home of the long-running manga 'Kochira Katsushika-ku Kameari Koen-mae Hashutsujo' (KochiKame). 15+ bronze statues of Ryotsu & co. are scattered around the station and Kameari Park, with themed manhole covers to hunt down. Plus the big Ario Kameari shopping mall (food, cinema, daily needs) and Kameari Katori Shrine — a proper slice-of-life 'downtown' Tokyo a single JR stop from your base.
activities.how_or_when: Kameari Station (JR Joban line) is one stop from Ayase / right by Towa — walkable or a 3-min train. Free; grab a statue map at the station and wander. Good first-day, jet-lag-friendly outing.
activities.area_or_park: Kameari, Katsushika (1 stop from Makoto Guesthouse)
activities.price_or_cost: Free (statues + shrine); mall as you like

activities.name: Shibamata — Taishakuten temple + Tora-san retro old-town
activities.detail: The most atmospheric old-Tokyo half-day near your base. A beautifully restored 17th-century Taishakuten temple covered in elaborate wood carvings, fronted by the Taishakuten Sando — a cobblestone shopping street of Showa-era snack shops, kusa-dango and tea (the setting of the beloved 'Otoko wa Tsurai yo / Tora-san' films). Add the Yamamoto-tei garden, the Tora-san museum, and the Yagiri-no-Watashi hand-rowed ferry across the Edo River.
activities.how_or_when: Keisei Kanamachi line to Shibamata (transfer at Keisei-Takasago) — ~20-25 min from your base. Temple grounds free; small fees for the garden/museum. Go mid-morning before the day-trippers; many sando shops close ~5pm.
activities.price_or_cost: Free temple; ~¥100-500 garden/museum; cheap street snacks

activities.name: Mizumoto Park — Tokyo's largest waterside park
activities.detail: A huge riverside park along the Edo River with metasequoia groves, lotus and iris ponds, long jogging/cycling paths, picnic lawns and lots of birdlife — a genuine escape from central-Tokyo crowds and a perfect calm reset while you're jet-lagged and flat-hunting.
activities.how_or_when: Bus from Kanamachi Station, or a long walk from Shibamata — easy to pair with a Shibamata morning. Free, open dawn-to-dusk. Best early morning; bring water in the July heat.
activities.price_or_cost: Free

activities.name: Tateishi — Nonbei Yokocho retro izakaya alley
activities.detail: One of Tokyo's last great Showa-era drinking warrens: a tangle of tiny standing bars and motsuyaki (grilled-offal) counters around Tateishi station, cheap and unpretentious, a true time-capsule downtown. Note it's partly under redevelopment — go while the old alley still stands.
activities.how_or_when: Keisei line to Tateishi — ~15-20 min from your base. Evenings; cash only, counters are tiny so arrive early (5-6pm) for a spot. Solo-friendly.
activities.price_or_cost: Cheap — ¥1,500-3,000 for a crawl

activities.name: Kita-Senju — your nearest big food/nightlife hub
activities.detail: The closest large hub to your base and the best default for dinner without trekking into central Tokyo: a buzzing student-and-old-town mix with dense izakaya, the old Nikko-kaido backstreets, department stores (Lumine, Marui) and some of the cheapest eats in the city. Surprisingly good night out for how little it costs.
activities.how_or_when: 1-2 stops on the Chiyoda / JR Joban line from Ayase. Anytime; evenings for the izakaya streets behind the west exit.
activities.price_or_cost: Budget-friendly

activities.name: Nishiarai Daishi (Sōji-ji) — a quiet major temple in Adachi
activities.detail: One of the Kanto region's 'three great Daishi' temples — a large, atmospheric Shingon complex with a five-storey-feel main hall, gardens, and old temple-town streets. A calmer, tourist-free alternative to Senso-ji, lively on festival/ennichi days.
activities.how_or_when: Tobu Daishi line — a 2-minute shuttle from Nishiarai Station — ~20 min from your base. Free grounds; mornings are serene.
activities.price_or_cost: Free

activities.name: Ghibli Museum (Mitaka) — lottery-style monthly ticket drop
activities.detail: Intimate Miyazaki/Studio Ghibli museum in Mitaka, west Tokyo (~25 min from Shinjuku). Date- and time-slot-specific, no same-day tickets, sells out within minutes. Strict no-photos inside; exclusive short film in the Saturn Theater. A must for the anime/tech-culture interest, and a quick half-day rather than a full day trip.
activities.how_or_when: Tickets via Lawson Ticket only. Released 10:00 JST on the 10th of each month for the FOLLOWING month (e.g. buy Aug 10 for Sep). Foreigners can use the English Lawson page; ticket carries the lead visitor's passport name and ID is checked at entry. Set a phone alarm for 09:55 JST on the 10th and be logged in early. Four entry slots: 10:00 / 12:00 / 14:00 / 16:00.
activities.price_or_cost: Adult ¥1,000 (cheap; the scarcity is the cost, not the price)

activities.name: Ghibli Park (Aichi) — advance-reservation overnight trip
activities.detail: Full theme park near Nagoya (Aichi Expo site): Grand Warehouse, Valley of Witches (Howl's castle, Kiki's bakery), Mononoke Village, Dondoko Forest. Bigger and newer than the Mitaka museum. ~1h40 by Shinkansen Tokyo→Nagoya then ~30–40 min to Aichikyuhaku-kinen-koen; realistically an overnight, not a Tokyo day trip. The Grand Warehouse slot is the hardest to get.
activities.how_or_when: All tickets are advance reservation, no door sales. Official release 14:00 JST on the 10th of the month, TWO months ahead (e.g. tickets for August go on sale June 10). Lawson/official channel needs a Japanese address + Japanese card; as a WHV holder living in Tokyo you'll have both, OR use Klook/KKday/JTB which support English/foreign cards. Avoid the 27th (Aichi-resident priority cuts general stock). Verify exact monthly times closer.
activities.price_or_cost: Area tickets roughly ¥1,500–¥7,800 depending on areas/Grand Warehouse; plus ~¥11,000+ Shinkansen each way and a hotel night

activities.name: Grand Sumo — Ryogoku Kokugikan (Tokyo basho)
activities.detail: Watching a 15-day tournament (basho) at Ryogoku Kokugikan is a signature Tokyo experience. Three of the six annual basho are in Tokyo. Go early afternoon for atmosphere, or arrive ~15:00 for the top-division (makuuchi) bouts and the closing ring-entering ceremony. Cheap upper-deck chair seats vs splurge ringside masu boxes.
activities.how_or_when: 2026 Tokyo dates: Hatsu (January) basho Jan 11–25, 2026; Aki (September) basho Sep 13–27, 2026; the May (Natsu) basho also runs in Tokyo. Tickets sell fast — Jan tickets went on sale Dec 6, 2025; Sep tickets on sale Aug 8, 2026 (the May basho tickets typically open early/mid April). Buy via the official Ticket Oosumo site or buysumotickets.com. Verify the May 2026 dates closer.
activities.price_or_cost: Single upper chair seats from ~¥3,000–¥8,500; masu box seats ¥10,000–¥20,000+ per person

activities.name: teamLab Borderless (Azabudai Hills) — permanent
activities.detail: Immersive digital-art museum, the permanent successor to the old Odaiba Borderless. Wandering, boundaryless rooms where artworks move between spaces. Central location in the new Azabudai Hills complex. Strong fit for the tech-culture interest. Timed entry; reflective/light-colored clothing recommended for the mirror rooms.
activities.how_or_when: Advance timed-entry only, no on-site sales. Book on the official teamLab site, Klook or GetYourGuide ~2–3 weeks ahead for weekends/sunset slots. Open year-round.
activities.price_or_cost: From ~¥3,800 (dynamic pricing — weekends/peak higher)

activities.name: teamLab Planets (Toyosu) — go before it closes
activities.detail: The barefoot, wade-through-water teamLab venue in Toyosu — different from Borderless (water rooms, the floating-orchid garden, mirrored infinity spaces). Roll up your pants; you walk through knee-deep water. Currently slated to close at the END OF 2027, so prioritize it during your WHV year while it's still open.
activities.how_or_when: Advance timed tickets via official DMM store or Klook, book ~2–3 weeks ahead. Closure currently extended to end of 2027 — verify the closing date closer, as it has been pushed back before.
activities.price_or_cost: From ¥3,200 (dynamic pricing)

activities.name: Hakone loop — Mt Fuji, Owakudani & onsen (Hakone Free Pass)
activities.detail: The classic Fuji-view day trip / overnight: mountain railway to Gora, cablecar + ropeway over the sulfur vents of Owakudani (eat a black egg), pirate-ship cruise on Lake Ashi with Fuji behind it, the Hakone Open-Air Museum, and onsen at Hakone-Yumoto. Doable in a long day but better as a one-night ryokan stay. Clearest Fuji views in winter (Dec–Feb).
activities.how_or_when: Buy the Odakyu Hakone Free Pass from Shinjuku (covers round-trip + all 8 Hakone transport modes + discounts). Add the Romancecar limited express for a reserved, faster ride. Buy online via Odakyu's EMot/global site or at the Shinjuku ticket counter. Any season; go on a clear day for Fuji.
activities.price_or_cost: Hakone Free Pass ~¥6,100 (2-day from Shinjuku); Romancecar +~¥1,200 each way

activities.name: Nikko — Toshogu shrine & Kegon Falls (UNESCO)
activities.detail: Ornate, gold-leafed Toshogu Shrine complex (Tokugawa Ieyasu's mausoleum, the 'see/hear/speak no evil' monkeys, Yomeimon Gate) plus the dramatic Kegon Falls and Lake Chuzenji up the Irohazaka switchbacks. Big, full day. Spectacular autumn foliage (late Oct–early Nov). Premium SPACIA X limited express makes the ride part of the fun.
activities.how_or_when: Tobu Railway from Asakusa (~2h on SPACIA X / Revaty Kegon). Get the Tobu 'Nikko Pass All Area' (~¥4,780) if you want Kegon Falls + Lake Chuzenji buses; the cheaper 'World Heritage Area' pass (~¥2,000) covers just the shrines. Leave Asakusa 7–8am. Reserve limited-express seats in advance for foliage season.
activities.price_or_cost: ~¥2,000–¥4,780 transport pass; shrine entry ~¥1,600

activities.name: Kamakura — Great Buddha, Enoden coast & bamboo temple
activities.detail: Seaside ancient-capital day trip: the bronze Great Buddha (Daibutsu) at Kotoku-in, Hasedera's gardens and sea views, Hokokuji's serene bamboo grove with matcha, Tsurugaoka Hachimangu shrine, snack-hunting on Komachi-dori, and the nostalgic Enoden train hugging the coast toward Enoshima. Easy, cheap, no advance booking needed.
activities.how_or_when: JR Yokosuka Line from Tokyo/Shinjuku Station (~60 min, ~¥920). Take the Enoden 3 stops to Hase for the Buddha. Consider the Enoden 1-day 'Noriorikun' pass if hopping stops. Year-round; hydrangeas at Hasedera in June, autumn colors at Hokokuji.
activities.price_or_cost: ~¥3,000–4,000 total day (JR return + Great Buddha ¥300 + Hasedera + konbini lunch)

activities.name: Kawagoe — 'Little Edo' half-day
activities.detail: Edo-era warehouse (kurazukuri) streets, the Toki no Kane bell tower, Kashiya Yokocho candy alley and sweet-potato treats — a compact, low-cost retro-Japan half-day that pairs well with renting a kimono. Closer and quicker than most day trips, good for a relaxed weekend morning.
activities.how_or_when: Tobu Tojo Line from Ikebukuro (~30 min express) or Seibu Shinjuku Line. Optional Tobu 'Kawagoe Discount Pass' bundles the train + local bus loop. No reservations needed; go on a weekday to dodge crowds.
activities.price_or_cost: ~¥1,000–1,500 round-trip; attractions mostly free or a few hundred yen

activities.name: Mt Takao — easy half-day hike with cablecar
activities.detail: Tokyo's favorite mountain, ~1 hour from Shinjuku. Cablecar or chairlift takes you halfway, then Trail 1 (~50 min, paved/gentle) leads past Yakuoin temple to the 599m summit with Fuji views on clear days. Great low-effort nature break, soba and tengu lore at the top. Autumn foliage and New-Year sunrise are peak draws (and peak crowds).
activities.how_or_when: Keio Line semi-limited express from Shinjuku to Takaosanguchi (~50 min). The Keio 'Takao 1-Day Ticket' (~¥1,690) covers the round-trip + cablecar/chairlift. No booking needed. Go early on clear autumn days; avoid late afternoon last-cablecar rush.
activities.price_or_cost: ~¥1,690 Keio 1-day ticket (incl. cablecar); train-only ~¥430 each way

activities.name: Street go-kart through Tokyo (Akihabara/Shibuya) — bring your Canadian IDP
activities.detail: Costumed go-karts driving real Tokyo streets past Tokyo Station, Ginza, Shibuya Scramble or the Rainbow Bridge — a bucket-list novelty fitting the games/arcade vibe. CRITICAL Canadian gotcha: you need a valid driving license PLUS an International Driving Permit. Canada is a 1949 Geneva Convention country, so a Canadian IDP works directly — but the IDP CANNOT be issued in Japan, so get it from CAA in Canada BEFORE you fly (it's valid 1 year). Note: a Japanese-issued license also works once you have one, but the IDP is the simplest route. No original docs at the shop = no drive, no refund.
activities.how_or_when: Book Street Kart (kart.st) or similar via their site, Klook or Viator a few days ahead. Bring your physical Canadian license + physical IDP. Tours run day and night; night runs through Shibuya/Tokyo Tower are the photogenic pick.
activities.price_or_cost: ~¥7,000–10,000 for ~1–2 hours; costume rental usually included

activities.name: Observation decks — Shibuya Sky, Tokyo Skytree, Tokyo City View
activities.detail: Three signature city-view spots. Shibuya Sky: open-air rooftop at 229m, no glass overhead, best ~30 min before sunset over the Scramble. Tokyo Skytree: Japan's tallest at 634m, Tembo Deck (350m) and Tembo Galleria (450m) with glass floors. Tokyo City View (Mori Tower, Roppongi, 52F): best photogenic angle on Tokyo Tower and, on clear winter days, Fuji — often bundled with the Mori Art Museum.
activities.how_or_when: Shibuya Sky: book a timed slot online (¥2,200 online vs ¥2,500 door); sunset slots sell out — book days ahead. Skytree: pre-book to skip lines, open 10:00–21:00. Mori Tower City View: usually walk-up. Clear winter afternoons give the best Fuji odds.
activities.price_or_cost: Shibuya Sky ¥2,200 online; Skytree ~¥2,100–3,400; Mori Tower City View ~¥2,000 (often incl. Mori Art Museum)

activities.name: Onsen-town escapes — Atami, Hakone-Yumoto, Kusatsu
activities.detail: For seasonal hot-spring trips: Atami is the fastest (seaside retro resort, ~40 min by Shinkansen from Tokyo Station) and great as a day trip; Hakone-Yumoto pairs onsen with the Fuji loop; Kusatsu (Japan's premier sulfur onsen, the steaming yubatake field) is ~2.5h by JR bus and best as an overnight, especially in winter snow. Many ryokan offer day-use (higaeri) bathing if you don't stay over.
activities.how_or_when: Atami: Tokaido Shinkansen Kodama/Hikari from Tokyo. Hakone-Yumoto: Odakyu Romancecar from Shinjuku (~1h25). Kusatsu: JR bus from Tokyo/Shinjuku, reserve ahead. Best in autumn (Oct–Nov foliage) and winter; outdoor (rotenburo) baths shine in the cold. Tattoos can be an issue at some baths — check policy or pick tattoo-friendly spots.
activities.price_or_cost: Day-use onsen ~¥1,000–2,500; transport ¥2,000–6,000 each way; ryokan overnight ¥12,000–30,000+ pp with meals

activities.name: Tokyo Disney Resort (DisneySea / Disneyland) — date-based tickets & app
activities.detail: DisneySea (the more adult/unique park, with the new Fantasy Springs Frozen/Tangled/Peter Pan area) and Disneyland. Date-specific dated tickets with dynamic pricing; weekday off-peak is cheaper and far less crowded. Use the official Tokyo Disney Resort app on the day for Standby Pass, Priority Pass and paid Premier Access to skip the worst queues. A full day each; go on a weekday given your year-long flexibility.
activities.how_or_when: JR Keiyo/Musashino Line to Maihama (~15–20 min from Tokyo Station). Buy dated tickets in advance on the official site/app — popular dates and Fantasy Springs sell out. Prices vary by date; cheapest on quiet winter weekdays.
activities.price_or_cost: 1-day 1-park ~¥7,900–10,900 depending on date (dynamic pricing)

activities.name: Toneri Park + Nippori-Toneri Liner ride
activities.detail: Adachi's biggest park — ponds with carp and ducks, sports fields, wide lawns — reached by the Nippori-Toneri Liner, a driverless elevated train that's a fun, scenic ride in itself. Pair it with the nearby Adachi Park of Living Things (生物園), a small butterfly house and petting zoo. A good jet-lag-friendly, low-key outing.
activities.how_or_when: Nippori-Toneri Liner to Toneri-kōen Station. Park free; Living Things park a small fee. Daytime.
activities.price_or_cost: Park free

building.name: WeWork All Access Plus (membership) + WeWork day pass (drop-in)
building.detail: The flagship gaijin-friendly option with the densest Tokyo network (40+ buildings: Shinjuku, Shibuya, Roppongi, Marunouchi, Iidabashi, etc.). All Access Plus lets you hot-desk at ANY WeWork in Japan (and worldwide) — ideal if you move around the city or travel within Japan. English-speaking community team, reliable fast wifi, free coffee/tea, printing, phone booths for your Canada calls, and frequent member networking events. For occasional use, buy single 'WeWork Day Pass' bookings via the app instead of committing monthly.
building.how_or_when: Sign up at wework.co.jp/en. Book day passes or tour via the WeWork app. No Japanese needed. Bring residence card / passport for first visit.
building.area_or_park: Network across Tokyo (Shinjuku, Shibuya, Roppongi, Marunouchi, Iidabashi, Ginza)
building.price_or_cost: All Access Plus ~JPY 42,900/mo tax incl.; single day passes typically ~JPY 3,000-5,000 booked in-app (verify current rate)

building.name: fabbit (drop-in friendly coworking chain)
building.detail: Budget-friendly Japanese coworking chain that genuinely welcomes drop-ins — the best 'just need a desk today' option. Locations include Kyobashi, Otemachi, and others. Quiet, clean, reliable wifi and power, good for heads-down dev work. Less of an international scene than WeWork but far cheaper for casual use. Good fallback when you don't want a monthly commitment.
building.how_or_when: Walk in or reserve via fabbit site. Some locations English-light, so use translation app. Best for occasional desk days.
building.area_or_park: Kyobashi, Otemachi and other central Tokyo nodes
building.price_or_cost: One-day pass around JPY 2,200/day at Kyobashi (verify per location); monthly plans available

building.name: MIDORI.so (Nakameguro / Ikejiri / Nagatacho / Bakuroyokoyama)
building.detail: The creative/design-leaning community space — ivy-covered renovated buildings, art gallery, cafe, weekly community lunches and workshops. Strong international, creative-professional crowd (designers, founders, indie makers), which fits your music-gear/anime/maker interests better than a corporate tower. More 'community' than 'office'. Pay-as-you-go option makes it easy to trial before committing.
building.how_or_when: Tour/apply at midori.so/en. English-friendly. Start with a pay-as-you-go day to feel out the community.
building.price_or_cost: Pay-as-you-go ~JPY 3,300/day or JPY 33,000 for an 11-day pack; Basic membership ~JPY 29,700/mo; full from ~JPY 42,350/mo; private booths from ~JPY 71,500/mo + JPY 11,000 admission

building.name: CIC Tokyo (Toranomon Hills Business Tower, 15-16F)
building.detail: Japan's largest innovation center and the single best place to plug into the Tokyo startup/dev ecosystem — ~280 startups, VCs, mentors, and corporates under one roof. This is where Venture Cafe's weekly 'Thursday Gathering' (free community networking) and many tech/startup events happen. Even if you don't take a desk, you can attend events here. Treat it as your community anchor, not just an office. Full coworking memberships are pricey/team-oriented; the value for a solo WHV dev is the events and network.
building.how_or_when: For events: register free via Venture Cafe Tokyo (venturecafeglobal.org) Thursday Gatherings. For desk/office: contact jp.cic.com/en. Go for the network even on a budget.
building.price_or_cost: Coworking/office is enterprise-priced (private rooms from ~JPY 200,000/mo); BUT Venture Cafe Thursday Gathering events are typically FREE to attend

building.name: Tokyo Metropolitan Central Library (Hiroo / Arisugawa Park)
building.detail: The single best FREE work spot in Tokyo for focused remote work. Free fast wifi (~140 Mbps, no time limit), ~300 seats WITH power outlets (~600 more without), huge English-language section, quiet, reservable individual research desks and a 5F group study room, plus an affordable cafeteria with a park view. Sits in leafy Arisugawa Park. Perfect for deep-focus dev days and Canada-overlap evening calls don't apply here (closes evening) but unbeatable for daytime cost of zero.
building.how_or_when: Just walk in during opening hours (closes evenings, some Mondays/holidays — verify on library.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/english). Arrive early on weekends for power seats.
building.price_or_cost: Free (no membership needed to enter and use; bring ID). Cafeteria meals cheap.

building.name: Musashino Place (free modern library/work space, Musashisakai)
building.detail: If you settle west/central Tokyo, this is a standout free public 'third place' — light-filled modern architecture, free wifi, plentiful power outlets, study/co-working zones, and a small cafe. Far more pleasant and design-forward than a typical library. Great free alternative to paid coworking on days you want quiet ambience without spending.
building.how_or_when: Walk in during opening hours (verify schedule). Good base if you live along the Chuo line.
building.price_or_cost: Free to use; cafe drinks cheap

building.name: Work-friendly cafe shortlist: Caffice, FabCafe, LATTEST, The Bridge, kissaten Renoir
building.detail: For ad-hoc work between meetings: Caffice (Shinjuku) is explicitly a 'cafe-meets-office' with free wifi and laptop-friendly seating; FabCafe (Shibuya/Hibiya) is a maker/tech cafe with abundant outlets and free wifi (fits your hardware/synth interest); LATTEST (Omotesando) has USB charging at every table; The Bridge (above Harajuku Station) has good wifi and plugs; kissaten Renoir (many central locations, e.g. Ginza) is a retro chain where you can camp for hours undisturbed with outlets. Note many indie Tokyo cafes discourage long laptop sessions and some lack outlets — these specific ones are safe bets.
building.how_or_when: Drop in. Buy a drink, ask/look for outlet seats. Avoid camping at tiny indie kissaten during busy hours. Renoir/Tully's/Doutor chains are the reliable fallback citywide.
building.area_or_park: Shinjuku, Shibuya, Hibiya, Omotesando, Harajuku, Ginza
building.price_or_cost: Cost of a drink (~JPY 500-700); some (Caffice) have time/per-use pricing — check on arrival

building.name: Canada<->Japan timezone reality for async remote work
building.detail: Tokyo is JST (UTC+9, no daylight saving). In summer Tokyo is 13h ahead of Toronto (EDT) and 16h ahead of Vancouver (PDT); in winter it's 14h ahead of Toronto (EST) and 17h ahead of Vancouver (PST). Practical reality: your Tokyo MORNING (e.g., 8-11am JST) overlaps with the previous Canadian afternoon/evening — that's your live-meeting window. A 9am ET Toronto standup = 10pm JST same day; a Vancouver 9am PT = 1am JST. Plan for genuinely async work: do your synchronous calls early-morning or late-evening JST, and keep the rest async (written updates, recorded Looms, clear handoffs). This 'follow-the-sun' offset is actually a selling point — you can deliver work overnight for Canadian colleagues. Block your calendar so you don't get pulled into 11pm-2am JST meetings daily.
building.how_or_when: Anchor live overlap to early-morning JST (overlaps Canada afternoon) or late-evening JST. Use a world-clock tool and protect sleep. Confirm exact offset around DST changeovers (Canada springs forward early/mid-March, falls back early November; Japan has no DST).

building.name: Connectivity #1: Japanese SIM/eSIM after you get your Residence Card (best value)
building.detail: On a 12-month WHV you'll have a Residence Card (zairyu card) — get a proper resident MVNO plan, not a tourist SIM, for the best price. IIJmio (Docomo network) offers ~3-55GB plans from roughly JPY 1,000-1,500/mo and is among the cheapest, but has little English support. Once settled, compare Rakuten Mobile, ahamo, LINEMO, UQ mobile, povo. Most require a Japanese address, Residence Card, and a Japanese bank account or credit card — so set up banking first. This is your primary, cheapest line for the year.
building.how_or_when: Apply after you have Residence Card + Japanese bank/credit card. IIJmio/Rakuten online; carriers in-store. Gotcha: many MVNOs need a Japanese payment card — get a bank account (e.g., Japan Post / Sony Bank / Rakuten) or a card first.
building.price_or_cost: IIJmio from ~JPY 1,000-1,500/mo for several GB; carrier plans (ahamo/LINEMO) ~JPY 2,000-3,000/mo for 20-30GB

building.name: Connectivity #2: English-support bridge SIM (Sakura Mobile / Mobal) for week 1
building.detail: For your first weeks before banking is set up, use an English-support resident SIM so you have a phone number for apartment/bank/utility sign-ups. Sakura Mobile gives full English support (Shinjuku office, airport counters, chat) — ~JPY 3,278/mo for 5GB, ~JPY 4,378/mo for 30GB. Mobal provides a voice+data eSIM WITH a Japanese phone number (essential for verifications) and no Residence Card required to start. More expensive than IIJmio, but the English support + immediate Japanese number removes week-1 friction; switch to a cheaper MVNO once settled.
building.how_or_when: Order before you fly; pick up eSIM/SIM at NRT on arrival 2026-06-30. Use it to get a Japanese number for bank/apartment, then port or switch to IIJmio/carrier later.
building.area_or_park: Airport pickup at NRT / Shinjuku office
building.price_or_cost: Sakura Mobile ~JPY 3,278/mo (5GB) to ~JPY 4,378/mo (30GB); Mobal voice+data plans from ~USD 11.50

building.name: Connectivity #3: Home internet + backup for reliable client calls
building.detail: For video calls with Canada you want wired stability, not just mobile. Many Tokyo apartments come with building fiber you can activate quickly; otherwise a no-contract pocket-wifi or home router (e.g. Rakuten Turbo / WiMAX-type) is a fast stopgap while fixed fiber (NURO/au/SoftBank) is installed — fiber installs can take 2-6 weeks. Keep your phone plan with enough data + tethering as call backup. A wired Ethernet adapter for your laptop noticeably improves call reliability versus shared apartment wifi.
building.how_or_when: Activate building fiber day one if available; order pocket-wifi as interim. Book fiber install early (long lead time). Share houses often include wifi — test its speed/upload before committing to client calls.
building.price_or_cost: Fiber ~JPY 4,000-6,000/mo; pocket-wifi / home router ~JPY 4,000-5,000/mo no-contract; Ethernet adapter ~JPY 1,500 one-time

building.name: Where the dev/startup community gathers (your networking plan)
building.detail: Plug in fast via these regulars: (1) Venture Cafe Tokyo 'Thursday Gathering' at CIC Tokyo/Toranomon Hills — free, weekly, the biggest open innovation mixer. (2) TokyoDev community (Paul McMahon) + Tokyo Rubyist Meetup — friendly, English, dev-focused talks and the best job board for foreigners in Japanese tech. (3) Tokyo Tech Meetup — international, quarterly. (4) ProductTank Tokyo — monthly, product/PM. (5) Le Wagon Tokyo — frequent free talks/workshops. (6) Builders Weekend — 48h hackathon (next edition late Mar-early Apr 2026) great for meeting builders fast. Track everything on dev.events/meetups/AS/JP/Tokyo and Meetup.com. As a solo remote dev, these are how you avoid isolation and find collaborators for your music-gear/games side projects.
building.how_or_when: Register: Venture Cafe Thursday Gathering (venturecafeglobal.org), TokyoDev.com newsletter/community, Meetup.com (Tokyo Tech Meetup, ProductTank Tokyo), dev.events for the full calendar. Start the first month — momentum matters.
building.price_or_cost: Most meetups free or ~JPY 1,000-2,000; hackathons sometimes a small fee

building.name: Co-ba (community-driven coworking network)
building.detail: Co-ba is a long-running Japanese community-coworking brand (Shibuya and other branches) oriented toward freelancers, creators, and small startups rather than corporate tenants — a friendlier, cheaper, more local-community feel than WeWork. Good middle option if WeWork is too pricey/sterile and you want to meet Japanese indie makers and founders. Branch availability and pricing vary, so check the specific location.
building.how_or_when: Tour the Shibuya branch; check current branches and plans on the co-ba site. More Japanese-language than WeWork — translation app helps.
building.price_or_cost: Monthly memberships vary by branch (roughly JPY 16,000-25,000/mo typical for community coworking); verify per location

building.name: WHV remote-work money gotchas (tax, pension, proof of funds)
building.detail: Critical for a Canadian WHV doing remote dev: (1) PROOF OF FUNDS — the WHV application requires showing sufficient funds (commonly cited around CAD 2,500+ plus return airfare, or more without a ticket) — have bank statements ready. (2) TAX — once you're a Japanese tax resident, income (including some remote earnings) can be taxable in Japan; Canada and Japan have a tax treaty to avoid double taxation, but you should confirm your situation with a tax professional and check CRA residency rules (you may become a non-resident or factual resident of Canada). (3) PENSION — if you enrol in Japan's pension system, you may be eligible for a Lump-sum Withdrawal Payment when you leave (claim within 2 years of departure); a Canada-Japan social security agreement lets you coordinate contributions. (4) Working Holiday visa generally allows work to supplement travel — confirm current rules on remote work for a foreign (Canadian) employer with the embassy. Mark all specifics 'verify closer' as rules and thresholds change.
building.how_or_when: Verify proof-of-funds amount on the Japanese Embassy in Canada site before/at application; consult a cross-border tax advisor after arrival; claim pension lump-sum within 2 years of leaving Japan. Verify closer — figures change.
building.price_or_cost: Proof of funds ~CAD 2,500+ (verify current requirement); pension lump-sum refundable on departure; tax varies

music.name: Ochanomizu Guitar Street (Meidai-dori / Gakkitengai)
music.detail: Tokyo's guitar/gear district: ~50 instrument shops clustered along Meidai-dori next to Ochanomizu Station. New, vintage and heavily-discounted used guitars, basses, amps, effects/pedals from every major brand (Fender, Gibson, Gretsch, Rickenbacker, PRS). Shops are packed close so price-comparison is easy. This is your home base for stringed gear and the easiest single afternoon to scope the whole scene.
music.how_or_when: JR Chuo/Sobu Line or Tokyo Metro Marunouchi Line to Ochanomizu Stn — street is at the exit. Most shops 11:00-20:00. Weekday afternoons quietest.
music.price_or_cost: Free to browse; used guitars from ~¥10,000 to vintage 6-figures.

music.name: Shimokura / Shimokura Second Hands (Ochanomizu)
music.detail: Anchor chain on Guitar Street. Good first stop on the street for used stringed gear and to gauge market prices before buying elsewhere.
music.how_or_when: Steps from Ochanomizu Stn on Meidai-dori. See access map on their site.

music.name: Miki Gakki (Ochanomizu)
music.detail: Osaka-based national chain with a strong Ochanomizu presence (including a 'Smalls' boutique guitar shop). Wide selection across guitars, amps and effects; part of the Ochanomizu cluster so easy to combine with the rest of the street. Note Miki Gakki also historically ran wind/band-instrument and pro stores — the Ochanomizu locations are guitar-focused.
music.how_or_when: ~4-min walk from JR/Metro Ochanomizu Stn. Typical hours ~11:00-20:00.
music.price_or_cost: Free to browse; new and used stock across price tiers;

music.name: Five G Music Technology (synth mecca)
music.detail: Legendary synth shop near Harajuku/Shibuya — Tokyo's single best destination for vintage AND modern synthesizers: classic analog mono/polysynths, modern keyboard synths, drum machines, plus a well-known Eurorack wall. Major Dave Smith Instruments/Sequential dealer. Staff repair and refurbish vintage units in-house, so vintage stock turnover can be slow and prices are fair-not-bargain. Treat it as a pilgrimage; serious vintage hunters should call/check stock before going.
music.how_or_when: Walk from Harajuku/Meiji-jingumae or Shibuya. Confirm current hours/address via shop before visiting; verify closer to your trip.
music.price_or_cost: Free to browse; used/vintage synths typically ¥50,000-¥500,000+. Not a bargain shop.

music.name: Rock oN Company (Shibuya)
music.detail: Pro audio / music-production specialist (est. 1989) in Jinnan, Shibuya. Best in Tokyo for DAWs, audio interfaces, monitors, controllers, plugins and studio gear — they've shifted from old analog synths toward pro production gear in recent years. Consultative, proposal-based shopping; good for kitting out a home/remote studio. English-friendly enough for browsing.
music.how_or_when: 1-8-18-1F Jinnan, Shibuya-ku. Open ~12:00-19:00, closed Sundays and irregular holidays. ~7-min walk from Shibuya Stn.
music.price_or_cost: Free to browse; gear from entry-level interfaces (~¥15,000) to pro monitors/converters.

music.name: Clockface Modular — 'Hatagaya Patching Center' showroom
music.detail: Japan's leading Eurorack-focused dealer (online since 2014) with a physical showroom you can visit to patch and audition modules before buying. Carries international Eurorack brands plus boutique Japanese makers including Tokyo Tape Music Center (Buchla-inspired modules). The single most useful stop for eurorack/modular in Tokyo. Showroom visits may be appointment-based — email ahead.
music.how_or_when: Rm 1, Ritz Palacio, 8-4-701 Hatagaya, Shibuya-ku (7F). ~6-min walk from Hatagaya Stn (Keio New Line) or Sasazuka Stn (Keio Line). Email/check site for showroom hours/booking; verify closer.
music.price_or_cost: Free to visit/audition; individual modules typically ¥15,000-¥80,000+. A starter rack runs ¥150,000+.

music.name: Tokyo Tape Music Center (Buchla-style modules)
music.detail: Boutique Tokyo maker of Buchla-100-inspired Eurorack modules (Dual Sine/Sawtooth 158, Dual Square 144, Tokyo Gate, etc.) — a play on the San Francisco Tape Music Center. No public storefront; buy/audition their modules in person via Clockface Modular's showroom or order online. Worth seeking out if you want West-Coast-synthesis character with a local pedigree.
music.how_or_when: Order at tokyo-tape-music-center.com or audition at Clockface Modular's Hatagaya showroom. No standalone shop.

music.name: Disk Union — Shinjuku flagship (and branches)
music.detail: Japan's essential used-record empire. The Shinjuku flagship is a multi-floor building organized by genre (Japanese rock/indies in the basement, prog, Latin/Brazil, used rock CDs, indie/alt by floor) with a cafe/bar on 1F. Branches also in Ochanomizu, Shibuya, plus Yokohama/Saitama/Chiba. Deep crates for rock, jazz, electronic and rare Japanese pressings — dig for bargains, though desirable titles sell at market value. Pairs perfectly with the listening-bar scene.
music.how_or_when: Multiple shops near Shinjuku Stn east side; genre-specialist stores are separate buildings. Typically ~11:00-21:00. Check each branch's hours.
music.price_or_cost: Used LPs/CDs from a few hundred yen; rare pressings climb fast. Free to browse.

music.name: e☆earphone Akihabara (headphone/audio building)
music.detail: Japan's premier personal-audio store — an entire building on Akihabara's main street with 3,000+ headphones/earphones/IEMs you can freely demo across all price tiers, plus a CIEM (custom in-ear monitor) section, a Devialet hi-fi corner, and new + checked second-hand stock with trade-ins and repair. The best place in Tokyo to audition monitoring/listening gear for your remote-work studio.
music.how_or_when: Shintou Bldg, 4-7-1 (also listed 4-6-7) Sotokanda, Chiyoda-ku — on Akihabara's main drag, ~3-min walk from Akihabara Stn Electric Town exit. Typically ~11:00-20:00.
music.price_or_cost: Free to demo; gear from ¥2,000 earbuds to ¥500,000+ flagship/CIEM.

music.name: Hard Off (used gear / Junk corner) — Akihabara & Oizumi-Gakuen
music.detail: Nationwide recycle-shop chain and the budget hunter's secret for used synths, drum machines, audio gear, amps and oddball instruments — especially the 'Junk' corner where untested/imperfect items go cheap. Akihabara branch has a solid instrument selection; the Oizumi-Gakuen store is the largest in greater Tokyo for used audio/electronics. Reality check: resellers have driven prices up, so true steals are now rare but still possible. Great low-stakes weekend dig.
music.how_or_when: Akihabara branch near the station; Oizumi-Gakuen on the Seibu Ikebukuro Line. Hit the Junk section first. Stock is luck-of-the-draw — go often.
music.area_or_park: Akihabara / Oizumi-Gakuen (Nerima) and many suburban branches
music.price_or_cost: Junk-corner gear from a few thousand yen; working synths still cheaper than dedicated shops but no longer dirt-cheap.

music.name: Nakano Broadway music floors (Mecano + synthpop digging)
music.detail: Inside the Nakano Broadway mall (anime/toy mecca) sit niche music shops — notably Mecano, a vinyl/CD shop billed as the mecca of Japanese synthpop, tucked among the otaku stores. A fun overlap with your anime/tech-culture interests: dig for Japanese electronic/synthpop records while you're there for the rest of Broadway. Note: some long-standing synth retail in Broadway has come and gone, so treat specific shops as 'verify on arrival.'
music.how_or_when: ~5-min walk from Nakano Stn (JR Chuo/Sobu) via the Sun Mall arcade into Broadway, upper floors. Mall hours vary by shop (~12:00-20:00).
music.price_or_cost: Used records from a few hundred yen up; rarities higher. Free to browse.

music.name: Listening bars / jazz kissa pilgrimage (Bar Martha, Little Soul Cafe, SHeLTeR, DJ Bar Bridge)
music.detail: Tokyo invented the deep-listening bar (jazz kissa / ongaku kissa): hi-fi systems, walls of vinyl, near-silent listening. Best starting points in 2026: Bar Martha (Ebisu) for the classic quiet-listening experience; Little Soul Cafe (Shimokitazawa) for a deep 60s soul/funk collection; DJ Bar Bridge (Shibuya) for an easier, more social first-timer vibe; SHeLTeR (Hachioji) for a serious audiophile pilgrimage further out. A perfect low-key way to study Tokyo's music culture and listening-room acoustics.
music.how_or_when: Evenings; small rooms fill up. Respect listening etiquette (silence during tracks). Confirm each venue's current hours/charge before going — verify closer.
music.price_or_cost: Expect a cover/seat/music charge (varies by venue/event) plus drinks — budget ~¥1,500-¥4,000 per visit. Many enforce quiet and no-photo/no-talking rules.

music.name: Ableton Meetup Tokyo (maker/producer community)
music.detail: Recurring community meetup for electronic-music producers — talks and demos on synthesis, modular-minded software workflows, Ableton Live techniques and chance/generative improvisation, hosted at small Tokyo venues. The single most accessible recurring entry point into Tokyo's music-maker/producer community and exactly aligned with your software + synth interests. Follow on Resident Advisor / social for the next volume's date and venue.
music.how_or_when: Check Resident Advisor (ra.co) and Ableton Meetup Tokyo socials for the next date; events run periodically, usually evenings/weekends. Verify the upcoming 2026 dates closer.
music.price_or_cost: Typically a small door charge / drink minimum (often ~¥1,000-¥2,500); some volumes free. Verify per event.

music.name: Tokyo Festival of Modular (FoM) 2026
music.detail: Tokyo's flagship modular-synth festival: international live acts, manufacturer booths, workshops and a marketplace — a once-a-year gathering of the modular/Eurorack community. Excellent for meeting makers, trying new modules and tapping the scene. 2026 edition is reported around late November; concert venue has been ORD (~4-min walk from Daikanyama Stn). Treat the exact date/venue/price as unconfirmed until the official site/socials post 2026 details.
music.how_or_when: Reported late November 2026. Watch the official FoM site, Facebook (TokyoModularFestival) and YouTube for confirmed dates, venue and tickets — verify closer.
music.area_or_park: Daikanyama / Shibuya area (venue varies by year)
music.price_or_cost: Day/festival passes in past years roughly ¥3,000-¥6,000; workshops may cost extra. Confirm 2026 pricing.

music.name: WHV money gotcha: tax-free shopping + carrying gear home
music.detail: Canadian-WHV-specific note for gear buying: Japan's tax-free (10% consumption-tax exemption) is for SHORT-TERM 'temporary visitor' status only. A Working Holiday visa is a residence status, so you are NOT eligible for tax-free — not on landing day, not in your first weeks. Budget the full 10% on every synth/amp/interface.
music.how_or_when: Assume you pay the 10% consumption tax on all gear. Hunt used stock (Disk Union, second-hand shops) for real savings instead. Keep receipts only for your own records / carrying gear home.
music.price_or_cost: Plan for 10% consumption tax on purchases once you're a resident; possible Canadian import duty on return.

music.detail: A tiny psychedelic basement live house in Higashi-Koenji with painted walls and a fierce booking policy — garage, psych, punk and weirdo electronics most nights, and the classic first-gig venue for underground Tokyo bands.
music.how_or_when: Shows most nights, doors usually ~18:30-19:00; buy at the door for most gigs (¥2,000-3,000 + drink), check ufoclub.jp/schedule — it's small, so popular nights sell out.
music.name: U.F.O. Club

music.detail: The Loft Project's ~250-capacity basement that has anchored Shimokitazawa's band scene since 1991 (35th-anniversary gigs running through 2026) — sweaty, loud, and the best room in Tokyo to catch a rock band right before they break.
music.how_or_when: Gigs almost nightly, doors typically 18:00-19:00; check the Loft Project schedule page and reserve via the band or e+ for bigger names, walk-up works for weeknight multi-band bills.
music.name: Shimokitazawa SHELTER

music.detail: Shibuya's flagship 1,000-capacity, four-floor techno club with a serious sound system, lasers and a giant mirror ball — weekend lineups pull international techno and drum & bass headliners, the reliable big-room electronic night.
music.how_or_when: Open Fri/Sat (plus event nights) roughly 23:00-05:00; photo ID required (residence card works), advance tickets via RA are cheaper (~¥3,500 vs ¥5,000+ door), and it fills after 1:00.
music.name: WOMB

music.detail: The mothership of Tokyo record shopping: a full building of genre floors (plus satellite shops like the Punk Market nearby) of meticulously graded secondhand vinyl and CDs — the electronic/club-music floor alone can eat an afternoon.
music.how_or_when: Open daily ~11:00-21:00; start at the main building and work floor by floor, bring cash or IC, and check the ¥100-500 bargain bins — weekday mornings are quietest for crate-digging.
music.name: Disk Union Shinjuku

geek.name: Akihabara — Electric Town core (arcades, retro, gachapon, anime)
geek.detail: Your home base district for this whole pillar. Within a 10-min walk: Super Potato (retro), Mandarake Complex, GiGO arcades, Gachapon Kaikan, Radio Kaikan (Steins;Gate landmark), figure/doujinshi/synth shops, plus maid cafes and electronics. Best done as a full afternoon-to-night crawl; come on a weekday to dodge crowds. Note the otaku scene is shifting — some legacy arcades have closed (see GiGO item), so treat any single shop as 'verify it's still there'.
geek.how_or_when: Open daily; most shops 11:00–20:00. Exit at Akihabara Station Electric Town Exit. Free to wander; bring cash (many small shops are cash-only) plus an IC card (Suica/PASMO) for arcades.
geek.price_or_cost: Free to browse; spend what you want

geek.name: Super Potato Akihabara (retro game mecca)
geek.detail: The legendary 3-floor retro shrine: Famicom through Dreamcast carts, consoles, controllers, soundtracks and arcade boards. 3F–4F are sales floors; 5F is the 'Retro Ge-Sen' rooftop-style arcade with classic cabinets you can actually play. Prices on rare/boxed items have climbed with the retro boom, so it's as much a museum as a shop — but mid-tier carts are still gettable.
geek.how_or_when: Open daily ~11:00–20:00, near the Electric Town Exit. Just walk in. Cash preferred for the rare stuff.
geek.price_or_cost: Free entry; loose carts from a few hundred ¥, boxed rarities ¥thousands+

geek.name: GiGO Akihabara arcades (UFO catchers / crane games)
geek.detail: IMPORTANT UPDATE: the iconic GiGO Akihabara 'Building 1' (the old SEGA tower, a landmark since 1992) closed permanently in August 2025. GiGO still runs Buildings 2, 3 and 5 nearby — Building 3 is the go-to for freshly stocked crane-game prizes (anime figures, plush). This is your spot to learn the crane-game meta before hitting bigger arcades.
geek.how_or_when: Open daily, typically ~10:00–23:30. Load money onto an Amusement IC card at in-store machines (credit cards accepted there) and tap to play, or use coins. Verify which buildings are open before a special trip.
geek.price_or_cost: ¥100–200 per crane play; budget ¥1,000–3,000 to actually win something

geek.name: Taito Station & big arcade chains (rhythm/fighting/competitive)
geek.detail: For rhythm games (taiko, maimai, Chunithm, Sound Voltage), fighters, gunner/medal games and competitive cabinets, Taito Station and GiGO multi-floor arcades are the staple. Great recurring after-work outlet near wherever you settle. Akihabara, Shinjuku and Ikebukuro branches are the most stocked.
geek.how_or_when: Open daily, usually until ~23:30–24:00. IC-card tap-to-pay on machines; credit cards work at the charging kiosks. Just walk in.

geek.name: Nakano Broadway (Mandarake mothership + collectibles maze)
geek.detail: A vertical 4-floor warren of 300+ shops with the densest concentration of rare anime/manga goods in Tokyo. Mandarake alone runs 30+ specialty stores here (separate shops for figures, cels, doujinshi, vintage toys, idol goods) — the world's largest secondhand anime retailer. Quieter and cheaper than Akihabara for serious collecting; floors 2–3 are the core.
geek.how_or_when: Complex ~10:00–20:00 but individual shops vary (many noon–20:00, some open at 13:00). 5-min walk up the Sun Mall arcade from Nakano Station North Exit. Free entry.
geek.area_or_park: Nakano (JR Chuo/Tokyo Metro Tozai, ~5 min from Shinjuku)
geek.price_or_cost: Free to browse; collectibles ¥hundreds to ¥tens of thousands

geek.name: Gachapon Kaikan / Akihabara Gachapon Hall (capsule toys)
geek.detail: A single building with 500+ gachapon (capsule-toy) machines — anime characters, weird miniatures (tiny ramen bowls, office supplies, animals in awkward poses). The most efficient one-stop for the capsule-toy ritual. Akihabara has several gachapon halls; this is the flagship.
geek.how_or_when: Open daily, generally ~11:00–20:00 (Gachapon Hall later, ~22:00). Walk in. Bring ¥100 coins — machines are coin-operated; there are change machines on-site.

geek.name: Shibuya PARCO 6F — Nintendo TOKYO + Pokémon Center + Jump Shop + Capcom + Godzilla
geek.detail: Five flagship pop-culture stores on one floor: Nintendo TOKYO (Japan's first official Nintendo store), Pokémon Center Shibuya, Jump Shop (Shonen Jump — One Piece, Dragon Ball, etc.), Capcom Store Tokyo, and the Godzilla Store. The single most efficient stop for first-party gaming/anime merch. Nintendo TOKYO gets queues on weekends.
geek.how_or_when: PARCO open daily ~11:00–21:00. ~5-min walk from Shibuya Station. No ticket needed; on busy days Nintendo TOKYO may issue numbered/timed entry — check the in-mall signage or PARCO site that morning.

geek.name: Pokémon Center Mega Tokyo + Pokémon Cafe (Ikebukuro)
geek.detail: The largest Pokémon Center in Tokyo, inside Sunshine City — broader stock than the Shibuya store, plus the adjacent Pokémon Cafe (themed food, exclusive goods). Good to pair with the Sunshine City arcades/aquarium. There are 4 Pokémon Centers in Tokyo (also Tokyo Station, Skytree); this is the headline one.
geek.how_or_when: Center open daily ~10:00–20:00. The Pokémon Cafe is RESERVATION-ONLY via the official Pokémon Cafe site — book the moment slots open (they release on a rolling ~31-days-ahead basis and sell out fast). Center itself needs no booking.
geek.price_or_cost: Free entry to store; cafe meals ~¥1,500–2,500

geek.name: teamLab Borderless — Azabudai Hills (timed-ticket digital art)
geek.detail: The 'wandering, borderless' digital-art museum — rooms with no fixed map where artworks move between spaces. Different experience from Planets (this one is shoes-on, no water). Dynamic pricing by date/time; weekend evening slots sell out first. This is a permanent flagship (newer than Planets), so less time pressure than Planets/Gundam.
geek.how_or_when: Buy TIMED tickets up to ~2 months ahead on the official site (teamlab.art) — book there first; resellers like Klook can sell out faster. Aim for a weekday slot.

geek.name: teamLab Planets TOKYO — Toyosu (barefoot, water-wading digital art)
geek.detail: The barefoot, immersive one — you wade through knee-deep water and walk on mirrors/moss. Expanded significantly in early 2026 (added Athletic Forest, Future Park, bigger Catching & Collecting Forest). Officially extended through END OF 2027, but it has been extended before, so don't treat the date as urgent — still, it WILL close eventually. Wear/bring shorts (you roll up trousers) and skip white clothing (reflective floors).
geek.how_or_when: Book TIMED tickets in advance on the official site (teamlab.art/e/planets) — sells out on weekends. Closes end of 2027 (verify closer; subject to extension). Yurikamome to Shin-Toyosu, ~1 min walk.

geek.name: Odaiba — Unicorn Gundam statue + Gundam Base + Round1 (DiverCity)
geek.detail: The 19.7m life-size Unicorn Gundam outside DiverCity transforms between Unicorn/Destroy modes with light/sound shows (free). Inside: The Gundam Base Tokyo on 7F (the premier Gunpla shop, exclusive kits) and Round1 Stadium (arcade, bowling, karaoke, sports). TIME-SENSITIVE: the Unicorn Gundam statue's exhibition is set to conclude END OF AUGUST 2026 — go in July/early August if you want to see it.
geek.how_or_when: Statue viewable free anytime; transformation shows run on a daily schedule (check the unicorn-gundam-statue.jp site that day). Go before end of Aug 2026 for the statue. DiverCity ~10:00–21:00; Yurikamome to Daiba or Rinkai Line to Tokyo Teleport.
geek.area_or_park: Odaiba, Koto-ku (DiverCity Tokyo Plaza; Yurikamome/Rinkai Line)
geek.price_or_cost: Statue free; Gunpla kits ¥500–¥10,000+; Round1 pay-per-play

geek.name: Retro game street-crawl: BEEP, Friends, Tokyo Video Gamers, RETRO:G
geek.detail: Beyond Super Potato, a cluster of smaller retro specialists worth a half-day: BEEP (retro PCs, doujin hardware, oddities), Friends (Famicom-era carts and knickknacks), RETRO:G, and Tokyo Video Gamers — a retro gaming BAR where you can drink and play classic consoles for an unlimited-play cover. ('Warpzone' as a named Akihabara shop couldn't be confirmed in current listings — likely closed/renamed; these are the live equivalents.)
geek.how_or_when: Most open ~11:00/12:00–20:00 daily; Tokyo Video Gamers runs into the evening as a bar. Walk in. Cash recommended for shops.
geek.price_or_cost: Free entry; Tokyo Video Gamers cover ~¥1,000–2,000 incl. play

geek.name: Anime pilgrimage (seichi junrei): Suga Shrine + Akihabara landmarks
geek.detail: Top accessible 'seichi junrei' spots: the Suga Shrine staircase in Yotsuya (the iconic final scene of Your Name / Kimi no Na wa) — a real residential staircase you can photograph anytime; pair with the Shibuya scramble/rooftop spots from Weathering With You. In Akihabara, Radio Kaikan and the surrounding streets are core Steins;Gate locations. Cheap, walkable, photo-driven.
geek.how_or_when: Suga Shrine stairs are a public road, open 24h (be quiet — it's residential); shrine grounds ~9:00–17:00, optional ¥500 goshuin seal. Short walk from Yotsuya Station (JR Chuo/Sobu, Marunouchi Line). Akihabara spots anytime. All free.

geek.detail: The original otaku mall: 30+ Mandarake specialty shops spread over floors 2-4, with Mandarake Galaxy (2F) for retro video games and the upper floors for vintage toys, doujin and oddities — denser and cheaper hunting than Akihabara.
geek.how_or_when: Most Mandarake shops open 12:00-20:00 (some floors shuttered before noon), so go early afternoon on a weekday; budget 2-3 hours and check prices per-shop since each Mandarake unit prices independently.
geek.area_or_park: Nakano (north exit, end of Sun Mall arcade)
geek.price_or_cost: Free to browse; retro carts from a few hundred yen to collector prices
geek.name: Nakano Broadway (Mandarake floors)

geek.detail: The most crawl-worthy central Hard Off: multiple floors of secondhand electronics whose legendary 'junk' bins turn up old keyboards, mixers, turntables, samplers and ¥100 records — untested rather than broken, so synth bargains happen.
geek.how_or_when: Open daily roughly 10:00-21:00 in the Rock Building at Sotokanda 3-11-2; head straight to the junk floor, bring cash for small buys, and test battery-powered gear in-store if you can.
geek.price_or_cost: Junk-bin finds ¥100-3,000; working gear market-price minus
geek.name: Hard Off Akihabara 1st store

geek.detail: Tokyo's temple of retro arcade gaming: two floors of original-hardware cabinets on real CRTs — After Burner with the moving seat, ~25 Street Fighter cabs, Cave shmups, Metal Slug — mostly ¥100 a play, with regular fighting-game tournaments.
geek.how_or_when: Open daily 10:00-24:00; weekday afternoons are calm for casual play, evenings and tournament nights get serious — check their X/Twitter for event schedules before claiming a versus cab.
geek.name: Game Center Mikado (Takadanobaba)

geek.detail: Japan's legendary vintage-synth shop, a 4th-floor room near Harajuku Station stacked with Moogs, Rolands, modular walls and rare Japanese machines — half museum, half store, and everything is playable.
geek.how_or_when: Open afternoons (typically ~11:00-20:00, check fiveg.net before going); it's one Chiyoda-line ride from Ayase to Meiji-jingumae — ask before patching anything, and browsing is welcome even if you're not buying.
geek.name: Five G Music Technology

itinerary.title: Hakone — an onsen & autumn-leaves overnight
itinerary.note: A classic no-car Hakone loop from Tokyo, timed for early-November colour. Buy the Hakone Free Pass (from Shinjuku/Odawara) — it covers the Romancecar surcharge separately and the whole loop: Hakone Tozan railway, cablecar, Owakudani ropeway, and the Lake Ashi sightseeing ship. Times are typical operator schedules — check the board on the day, and note ropeway sections can pause for wind/volcanic gas. Alternatives to Hakone: Nikko (peak koyo late Oct) or Kawaguchiko (Fuji + maples).
